strengths: UniAP addresses a useful systems problem for computer vision: automatically choosing pipeline partitions and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies under hardware and memory constraints. Optimizing these interacting decisions together is a worthwhile direction.

Table 1 demonstrates meaningful measured improvements. On ENVB-8, ViT-Huge reaches 45.58 samples/s versus Alpa’s 38.74, and Swin-Huge reaches 19.08 versus Galvatron’s 13.90. Llama-7B achieves the reported 3.80× throughput improvement over Galvatron. Matching throughput while reducing planning time in other settings also has practical value.

The evaluation covers five Transformer families, including two vision architectures, and four hardware environments. Experiments extending to 64 DCUs provide useful weak-scaling evidence. Appendix E reports a 3.59% average throughput-estimation error for selected configurations, and the model specifications, solver settings, and topology case study improve transparency.
weaknesses: The stated constraints do not enforce pipeline precedence. For a graph u→v with two stages, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 satisfies the contiguity and placement constraints in Equations (6)–(7), but Equation (4) assigns zero communication cost to this edge. Thus, the formulation can favor placements with unaccounted communication. Appendix A proves contiguity, which does not establish the required stage ordering. This is a consequential correctness issue in the central formulation.

Equations (3)–(4) contain fourth-degree products of decision variables, such as P_ui P_vi S_uk S_vl, so the presented formulation is not directly an MIQP. These products can be reformulated using auxiliary variables, but the necessary linking constraints and actual solver formulation are absent. This omission is repairable, yet materially limits reproducibility and prevents checking whether the implemented optimization matches the stated method.

The memory-feasibility claim is insufficiently supported. Algorithm 1 constructs M using micro-batch size b=B/c, and Section 3.2 scales activation memory by that supplied batch size. GPipe without activation checkpointing retains activations from multiple micro-batches before backward execution, but the stated memory calculation does not account for this accumulation. No peak-memory validation resolves the discrepancy, which directly affects whether selected strategies are feasible.

The repeated optimality claims exceed the demonstrated guarantees. Appendix D specifies a 60-second solver limit and early termination with a relative gap below 4%, without reporting achieved gaps. Algorithm 1 also restricts stage counts and micro-batch counts to divisors of device and batch counts. The results therefore support approximate optimization within a restricted, estimated cost model. Treating the solver timeout as constant in Section 3.5 does not establish the complexity of obtaining an optimum.

The ablation does not isolate the claimed advantage over hierarchical optimization. Figure 6 compares joint optimization against inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only variants, whereas Alpa and Galvatron already combine both categories. A comparison using the same strategy space, cost model, execution backend, and resources is missing. Hierarchical decomposition alone does not imply suboptimality, so the blanket characterization of prior methods and attribution of gains to joint search remain insufficiently established.

Search-time comparisons exclude profiling, and Section 4.2 explicitly attributes part of the advantage to multithreaded Gurobi versus single-threaded baselines. The reported wall-clock improvements are useful, but matched-resource comparisons and an end-to-end setup-time breakdown are absent. Overall, the practical gains merit consideration, but the unresolved formulation and memory-feasibility issues, together with weak isolation of the central contribution, determine the weak-reject recommendation.
